text: The dashboard concept you already know -- a live view that answers what needs attention right now instead of summarizing the past -- has a specific implementation inside Sentinel, and it's called a workbook. Workbooks aren't a feature Microsoft built just for Sentinel. They're part of Azure Workbooks, a reporting framework that lives in Azure Monitor and is reused across many Azure services.

Sentinel surfaces that same framework under its own Workbooks page, pre-pointed at your Sentinel data. A workbook is assembled from a small set of building-block steps stacked on a canvas: a text step explaining what a section shows, a query step rendered as a table or chart, a parameter step like a dropdown or time-range picker, and a link step that jumps to another view.

A query step is where Chapter 2's KQL work pays off directly -- every chart and table in a workbook is backed by a real KQL query run against your Log Analytics workspace, the same workspace covered in Lesson 2. A parameter step is what turns a flat report into something you can steer: pick a different time range or hostname, and every step wired to it re-runs and updates in place.

That's the practical difference from a static dashboard screenshot. A screenshot answers one question frozen at one moment. A workbook answers a family of related questions, because an analyst can change a parameter and immediately see the same queries re-run against a different slice of data -- narrowing a sign-in workbook from the last 24 hours to the last hour, without touching a line of KQL.

That's the reason Sentinel leans on workbooks instead of static dashboards for investigation work: the person using one rarely wants the exact view its author first built. They want a starting point they can reshape live. Next up, Lesson 14 looks at where those workbooks actually come from -- Microsoft's built-in templates versus one you build yourself.
